stories.summary: In a ridiculously well-maintained office, Ajay was in mid-conversation, took an abrupt right turn, and crashed straight into a glass wall so spotlessly clean it was effectively invisible. He hurt himself. Amit jokes that the wall's clarity matches Ajay's prose, and then turns it into the framing metaphor of the episode — the state is similarly invisible most of the time, until it suddenly slams into your life.
stories.insight: We normalise the state's presence to the point of not noticing it — like fish unaware of water — until we collide with it through taxes, regulations, or police. The pain of the bump is what reveals the wall.

stories.topic: The Poker Stable and the Rare Player Who Asks Why
stories.summary: In Ajay's poker years, many young pros came up through 'stables' — a successful player would stake and coach a stable of juniors, drilling them on mechanics: with twenty big blinds, here is your reshove range, here is your equity in this spot. Most memorised the rules and played correctly without ever thinking from first principles. Only a tiny minority of the already-tiny minority of winning players ever stopped to ask why the rule was the rule. Ajay says he was always one of those askers.
stories.insight: The difference between a competent operator and a real master is the willingness to interrogate the mechanics. Memorised heuristics work in the world they were trained on; first-principles thinking lets you handle the world that hasn't arrived yet.

stories.summary: On his old blog India Uncut, Amit kept a running series called 'Where Your Taxes Go,' which catalogued where Indian state spending actually went — and which kept on going past number eighty. The list included mustache allowances for policemen, rehabilitating monkeys, overpaid condom contracts, a state company that also made sex toys, policing parrots, fake municipal employees drawing salaries, golf buggies for the army, sixty-two sandstone elephants, and the regulation of skirt hemlines.
stories.insight: Once you accept that tax money is extracted by coercion, the moral question of how it is spent becomes urgent. A frivolous expenditure isn't merely wasteful — it is funded by violence, and that gives every absurd line item a real ethical weight.

stories.topic: The Restaurant That Cannot Legally Exist
stories.summary: Amit recalls his early podcast episode with Madhu Menon, a Bangalore restaurateur, who explained that to run a restaurant in India you need a long list of licences — and the rules are mutually contradictory. The Excise department, wanting to track alcohol movement, demands that there be only one entry door. The Fire and Safety departments demand that there be multiple doors. It is mathematically impossible to comply with both, so every restaurant is by definition operating illegally and pays thirty to forty bribes a month to keep going.
stories.insight: Over-regulation in India is not about safety — it is about control and rent extraction. When laws are designed so they cannot all be obeyed, every business becomes a criminal by default, and the resulting bribes become an unbudgeted, unaccountable tax.

stories.topic: The UAE Official Who Could Enact a Law Tomorrow
stories.summary: Ajay was once sitting with a senior policymaker in the UAE discussing securities law. The official thumped the table and said, 'You give me the correct securities law tomorrow and I will have it enacted by the day after.' The intended boast — speed and decisiveness — struck Ajay as the opposite of strength.
stories.insight: If a law can be enacted overnight, it can be unenacted overnight. Frictionless legislative power is not the mark of a strong state but of an unsafe one — it abolishes legal certainty entirely. Liberal democracy's slow, deliberative ponderousness is a feature, not a bug.

stories.topic: America Was Founded by Mad Religious Sects
stories.summary: Ajay places early American political philosophy in its real historical context. America was settled in large part by religious sects fleeing persecution by mainline European Catholic and Protestant churches — not deviants in the modern sense of atheists, but deviants in the sense of crazier, more specialised religious sects than the European mainstream tolerated. The original meaning of 'separation of church and state' was therefore not the on-ramp to secularism we now read into it, but space for each crazy sect to live by its own rules. From this came a deep American instinct for communes, charter cities, and walled-off rule-sets, where 200 people might suspend large parts of the state's rule-set within their boundary.
stories.insight: The American genius for letting subgroups write their own rules — within universal limits like 'no murder' — is not a side effect of secularism but its forgotten origin. India would benefit from taking this question seriously: which parts of the state's monopoly can a self-organising community legitimately suspend, and which must always apply universally?

stories.summary: Ajay observes a striking historical inversion: the levels of taxation imposed by the British Raj that provoked Gandhi's Dandi March were actually modest and decent compared with the level of taxation in independent India. Indians have grown to accept usurious rates of taxation as normal.
stories.insight: What once provoked a national independence movement is now accepted without protest. The salt tax is an anchor for measuring how much state extraction we have normalised — and a reminder that outrage thresholds drift.

stories.summary: At the Orange City Literature Festival in Nagpur, an audience member asked Ajay whether he wanted India to be a tiger or an elephant. Ajay surprised himself by answering, 'I want us to be the tortoise.' The point was that a hundred years of slow, organic, deliberative growth — chipping away at modernity, making fewer mistakes, avoiding the temptation of dictatorship for speed — produces more durable success than a thirty-year sprint.
stories.insight: A 7% real per-capita GDP growth rate sustained for thirty years has essentially never happened in world history. The dream of catching up to the United States in one generation requires authoritarian shortcuts that destroy the very institutions you would need to be the United States. Better to be a tortoise and discover, rather than design, the path to a healthy society.

recommendations.item: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column for the Times of India arguing that the state, by its nature, exists through coercion — and that every action it takes is therefore funded by violence.
recommendations.reason: Establishes the moral frame for the entire episode. Whether you are libertarian, communist, or social democrat, you have to justify the violence — to say that for these particular ends, coercion is acceptable. Naming the cost is the first step to weighing it.

recommendations.item: Your Maid Funds Unani
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A 2007 piece arguing that everyone in India is a taxpayer — including the domestic worker buying salt and the beggar buying milk — because indirect taxes touch every transaction.
recommendations.reason: Demolishes the popular myth that 'only 3% of Indians pay taxes.' If the state spends violence-extracted money on, say, Unani medicine, it is your maid who is funding it. The moral cost of state spending is borne all the way down the income ladder.

recommendations.item: Taxes Should Be Used for Governance, Not Politics
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack piece arguing that since taxes are a coerced moral cost, they should be spent on the core protective functions of the state — not on political signalling.
recommendations.reason: Operationalises the 'every act of government is violence' frame: if the violence is justified for protecting rights, it is much harder to justify for statues and frivolous schemes.

recommendations.item: Where Your Taxes Go (India Uncut series)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's running blog catalogue of absurd government expenditures — from mustache allowances to sandstone elephants — assembled over years.
recommendations.reason: A running gag that doubles as a moral inventory. Each entry is a worked example of coerced money being spent on something whose justification under 'protecting individual rights' is, at best, strained.

recommendations.item: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
recommendations.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
recommendations.context: Bhadra's book on the over-reach of the Indian state and how it strangles ordinary lives.
recommendations.reason: The source of one of Amit's favourite frames: constitutions are contextual. The American constitution, born of religious refugees, was designed to protect people from the state. The Indian constitution, born in the violence of partition with the centre barely holding, was designed to protect the state from people. That inversion still shapes Indian governance today.

recommendations.item: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (Episode 333, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Subhashish Bhadra
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen and the Unseen conversation with Subhashish Bhadra around Caged Tiger.
recommendations.reason: The longer conversation around the contextual-constitution argument and the lived costs of an over-broad Indian state.

recommendations.item: State Building
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Fukuyama's slim book introducing the scope-and-strength framework for thinking about states.
recommendations.reason: The source of the central analytical frame Amit uses in this episode: states should be understood not as 'big' or 'small' but as a pair of dials — scope (how much they try to do) and strength (how well they do it). Limited scope plus high strength is the goal; India has the opposite.

recommendations.item: Restaurant Regulations in India (Episode 18, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Madhu Menon
recommendations.context: Amit's early Seen and the Unseen episode with the Bangalore restaurateur Madhu Menon.
recommendations.reason: The source of the 'one door vs many doors' contradiction. A worked example of how the Indian state's overgrown scope produces unfollowable rules and turns honest businesses into permanent bribe-payers.

recommendations.item: Going from Strong as in Scary to Strong as in Capable
recommendations.creator: Suyash Rai and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A Leap Blog essay distinguishing two very different meanings of 'strong state.'
recommendations.reason: Ajay's worked-out version of the central distinction in the episode: the bad meaning of 'strong' is a state that can grab the most powerful person in the country and put them in jail; the good meaning is a state that can deliver a polio-vaccination programme on schedule. India admires the first and needs the second.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive on the 1991 liberalisation reforms.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of the 1991-to-2011 hare-burst of Indian growth that the episode invokes — and of the subsequent slowdown the duo says shows we have not yet built the durable institutions of a tortoise.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the moral and practical case for freedom.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode that lays the groundwork for treating individual rights as the prior, and the state as the instrument that exists to protect them.

recommendations.item: Essays on Nationalism
recommendations.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
recommendations.context: Tagore's slim collection of essays critiquing the modern nation-state.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's main recommendation. Tagore is one of the most beautiful writers of the English language and his attack on the nation-state — its capacity to crush the individual and human brotherhood — is timeless. Short enough that the reader who complained 'I am too lazy to figure this out myself' has no excuse.

recommendations.item: The Libertarian Reader
recommendations.creator: David Boaz
recommendations.context: Boaz's anthology of classical-liberal essays from Milton Friedman, Friedrich Hayek and others.
recommendations.reason: Don't be put off by the label in the title — Amit urges readers to focus on principles rather than tribal labels. A clean distillation of how liberal thinkers across centuries have approached the question of what the state is for.

recommendations.item: What Is Libertarianism? (Episode 117, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with David Boaz
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen and the Unseen conversation with David Boaz.
recommendations.reason: The longer companion to the book recommendation — a chance to hear Boaz himself work through the ideas.

recommendations.item: The Origins of Political Order
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: First volume of Fukuyama's two-part magisterial history of the state.
recommendations.reason: Charts how states evolved from tribal bands to modern bureaucracies. Essential for understanding why some states cohere into Denmark and others fail into Somalia, and why the path matters more than the destination.

recommendations.item: Political Order and Political Decay
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Second volume of Fukuyama's history, taking the story into modernity.
recommendations.reason: The companion volume on how mature states decay — vital for understanding why getting institutional design right is a permanent project, not a one-time triumph.

recommendations.item: Kashi Ka Assi
recommendations.creator: Kashinath Singh
recommendations.context: A Hindi novel set in Banaras, the source of the phrase 'bhajai harmonia.'
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's family-friendly version — 'Bharme Jay Dunya, Hum Bhajai Harmonia.' A reminder that one is sometimes tempted to opt out of the world entirely and just play the harmonium — but if you care about society, you must understand the delicate interplay between state and citizen, and that requires engagement, not retreat.

recommendations.item: The Policy Questions Around Airlines
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's recent Substack/Mayin piece doing a deep dive on airline industry public policy as a worked example.
recommendations.reason: Ajay opens the episode by using the article to set up the tension between domain-specific case studies and first-principles frameworks. The article itself is the worked case that he says only becomes useful when paired with general principles.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE episode on the failures of Indian education and knowledge institutions.
recommendations.reason: Picks up the thread on the failure of liberal-arts education in India that Ajay returns to here — the diagnosis that the Indian middle class lacks the basics of liberal-arts thinking, which is why it admires 'strong leaders' in all the wrong ways.

recommendations.item: The Pune Public Policy Festival
recommendations.creator: Pune Public Policy Festival
recommendations.context: The episode's sponsor — a public policy festival in Pune on 19-20 January 2024 themed around 'tradeoffs.'
recommendations.reason: Pune was once the Oxford of the East and an intellectual hub of Indian discourse before the centre of policy gravity shifted to Delhi. The festival is an attempt to revive a more decentralised intellectual ecosystem and gathers young professionals with public-policy experts, bureaucrats, economists and thinkers around the unavoidable tradeoffs of modern governance.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's writing course.
recommendations.reason: Linked from the show notes; Amit's standing recommendation for anyone who wants to write more clearly.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on Indian economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Referenced as the larger framework for the next episode in the planned arc — when the state should make policy and what public policy actually means. The book Amit calls Ajay's 'masterpiece.'

core_ideas.concept: The Existence of the State Is Itself an Act of Violence
core_ideas.explanation: It is not just that some state actions are violent — the state itself is violence. The state is funded by taxes, and taxes are extracted under the threat of imprisonment. Nobody would pay if they could opt out. The state is, in Amit's framing, a 'monopoly mafia' to which we have agreed to submit because we need it to defend our rights. Whatever else it does, that fact remains: every rupee it spends is a rupee taken under coercion, and every act it commits is an act of violence. This is not an argument against the state; it is an argument that the state must always be justified, function by function, against the moral cost of the violence that funds it.
core_ideas.quote: Whatever the state does, it does through violence. And therefore you have to justify that.

core_ideas.explanation: Liberalism says we all have inviolable rights. But for those rights to have meaning, they must be defended — and defending them requires an entity with a monopoly on violence. So liberalism, the doctrine that no one should infringe your rights, requires the creation of an institution authorised to infringe everyone's rights at least a little. The trick is to keep that infringement minimal, scoped to the protection of the prior rights themselves.

If a third of your income goes in taxes — direct, indirect, milak, and everything else combined — then for four months of every year, from January to April, you are not working for yourself. You are working for the state. The frame is deliberately uncomfortable: the social contract is real, but so is the fact that if it is not delivering protection in return, you are providing forced labour without service.
core_ideas.quote: Between January and April every year, you don't work for yourself, you work for the state.

core_ideas.explanation: The popular Indian claim that 'only 3% pay taxes' is nonsense. Direct income tax is one slice; indirect taxes touch every transaction. The domestic worker buying salt is a taxpayer. The beggar at the traffic signal buying tea or milk is a taxpayer. Even inflation is a tax — when the government expands the money supply, prices rise, and the tax falls heaviest on the poor. The moral cost of state spending is borne by everyone, all the way down.

core_ideas.concept: The Two Channels of State Coercion
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's important refinement: the monopoly on violence operates through two channels. The first raises money (taxation, which is then spent on whatever the state has decided to do). The second is raw coercion — 'thou shalt not' rules backed by punishment. Crucially, the first channel has a budget constraint: rupees are rupees, raising them is hard, and politicians count them. The second channel has no budget constraint at all. There is no unified ledger of state coercions. Hundreds of agencies layer on new prohibitions every day, and citizens normalise each new loss of freedom. The hidden coercion may be the bigger public-administration problem precisely because nothing keeps it in check.
core_ideas.quote: There is no single statement that details and documents all the acts of state coercion.

core_ideas.explanation: Francis Fukuyama's two-axis frame for understanding states. Scope is the breadth of what the state attempts (defence and law-and-order at the minimum; up through infrastructure, temples, statues, space programmes, and skirt hemlines at the maximum). Strength is state capacity — the ability to actually deliver in whatever domains it has chosen. Sierra Leone is low scope, low strength — anarchy. The USSR was high scope, medium strength — totalitarian and inefficient. The ideal is limited scope, massive strength — a state that does few things but does them superbly. India is the worst of both worlds: high scope, low strength — interfering everywhere, accomplishing nothing well.

core_ideas.concept: Strong as Capable, Not Strong as Scary
core_ideas.explanation: There are two very different meanings of 'strong state' loose in Indian middle-class discourse. The bad meaning: the state is so badass it can grab the most powerful people in the country and put them in jail; or so unconstrained it can announce a brand-new law tomorrow. The good meaning: the state is competent enough to deliver a polio vaccination to every child, to handle a pandemic without disastrous death tolls. The first meaning is the dictator's swagger; the second is liberal-democratic state capacity. India tends to admire the first when it desperately needs the second.
core_ideas.quote: I am badass, I can grab anybody and put them in jail. I can do anything that I want and announce a brand-new law the day after tomorrow. These two conceptions of strong are writ large in the Indian conception — and I think they're just both wrong.

core_ideas.concept: The Slowness of Liberal Democracy Is a Feature, Not a Bug
core_ideas.explanation: The very words 'freedom' and 'liberal democracy' denote a ponderous, deliberative process of state action. Power must be dispersed; there should be no single decision-maker; checks and balances should make legislation slow, consultative, and shambolic — because anyone who can enact a law tomorrow can re-enact it the day after, which abolishes legal certainty. Robust institutions are designed so that even the worst person you can imagine, on coming to power, can do only limited damage.

Borrowed from Subhashish Bhadra's Caged Tiger. The American constitution emerged from religious refugees fleeing persecution — its mission was to protect people from the state, and it valorised individual freedom. The Indian constitution emerged from the violence of Partition, when the centre might not hold — its mission was to protect the state from the people, and it centralised power. That inversion is not a historical curiosity; it still shapes Indian governance, where the state behaves as if citizens exist for its sake rather than the other way around.

Amit's heroes from the Indian freedom struggle — Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Mahadev Govind Ranade, Gopal Krishna Gokhale — were all liberal in their ends but conservative in their means. They wanted a freer, more just society, but pursued it through engagement, dialogue and discourse, not through revolutionary overnight imposition. The same goes for liberalism today: if the state can impose liberalism on you tomorrow, it can impose gulags on you the day after. A liberal society must be discovered through a robust process of dialogue, not designed through a strongman's will.

Echoing Adam Ferguson's line about social progress as 'the result of human action but not of human design,' Amit and Ajay argue that the success of post-1991 India came from freeing pieces of the economy and letting positive-sum trades discover the path forward. You cannot bulldoze a country into modernity through a thirty-year sprint of 7% per-capita growth — that has essentially never happened in history without disastrous authoritarian shortcuts. Sustained 100-year growth like that of the UK and the US emerged organically through deliberation, fewer mistakes, and the long, slow chipping away that we mistake for tortoises losing the race.
core_ideas.quote: We organically discover, not design, what it means to be a healthy liberal society.

core_ideas.explanation: Two strategies for engaging the world: memorise the mechanics, or work from first principles. Most poker players in a stable memorise the heuristics — at twenty big blinds with this hand, here is your range — and they play correctly without ever asking why. The rare master always asks why. The same applies to engineering education (you can fix this air conditioner, or you can know thermodynamics well enough to invent the next one) and to the liberal arts (in which 'useless' general principles are the best preparation for the seventy years of working life that lie ahead of any twenty-year-old). Asking why is cumbersome; not asking why limits you to the world that already exists.

Two ways to convey ideas. A story grabs attention and lands a principle, but the principle is then 'adrift in space' — easily forgotten, like a LinkedIn lesson. A framework takes more effort to present but gives the listener a structure they can apply to anything new. Better still: the framework's flaws are visible and arguable, so the listener can engage with what really matters. Ajay confesses he is a first-principles person — economics, for him, is not the dismal science but a lens that explains all of human behaviour, from policy to art.

A live and underexplored question, embedded in American political philosophy from its founding: can a self-organising community of two hundred people draw a boundary wall around themselves and suspend portions of the state's rule-set inside? Some rules clearly cannot be suspended (the prohibition on murder must apply universally). But many can be — and the American tradition of charter cities, religious communes, and special jurisdictions is a long experiment in working out which is which. India would benefit from taking that question seriously rather than treating the state's rule-set as monolithic and total.

Ajay's distinction at the close. There is an instrumental objective: you want to do business, govern, change the world, and so you need to understand it. That is healthy and worthy. But there is also an amusement objective — you are alive, the spectacle is unfolding around you, and you will simply have more fun watching it if you understand it. Like a chess game: knowing more about chess does not change the game, but it changes your ride. Knowledge is partly a tool and partly a way of enjoying being here.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the glass wall Ajay walked into: 'In terms of clarity, there is something that is out there that can match the clarity of your prose. So compliments to both you and the glass wall.'
Ajay describing his own role in episode planning: Amit corrects him — 'I am the person who puts the I and V. I haven't envisioned anything. We have envisioned.'

Amit on the tortoise pace of a thirty-year sprint: 'A tortoise has a really long lifespan if I remember correctly. They can live up to a thousand years or something. So for them, thirty years sprint kind of makes sense.' Ajay's amendment: 'Two hundred, three hundred years.'

Amit's image of the Tortoise: 'Live with Hera, listen to Hindustani classical' — and Ajay's interjection: 'Listen to The Seen and the Unseen.' Amit: 'Listen to The Seen and the Unseen, but which is often heard by hares at double speed, which is also perfectly fine. We cater to hares, we cater to tortoises, and we cater to some human beings.'
Ajay on his fellow Bengali Tagore: 'My heart fills with joy that you named my fellow Bengali Robida, and I almost feel like you're flirting with me.'

Amit's closing tally: 'Did you ever think that there would be an episode of Everything Is Everything in which seven different animals would be mentioned. We've had a cat, a dog, a pig, a tiger, an elephant, a tortoise, and a hare.'
Ajay on his Pune-festival rebrand of India: when asked at the Orange City Lit Fest whether he wanted India to be a tiger or an elephant, he answered 'I want us to be the tortoise.'

David Boaz: 'Conservatives want to be your daddy, telling you what to do and what not to do. Liberals want to be your mommy, feeding you, tucking you in and wiping your nose. Libertarians want to treat you as an adult.'
Winston Churchill, quoted by Ajay as comic interruption: 'Dogs look up to us, cats look down on us, pigs treat us as equals.'
Adam Ferguson on social progress as 'the result of human action but not of human design' — invoked by Amit to underline 'discover, not design.'

Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi, family-friendly version: 'Bharme jaye duniya, hum bhajai harmonia.' Roughly: 'The world can go to hell — I'll just play the harmonium.' Ajay's standing temptation, which he resists in the name of engagement.

Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia is namechecked as the great philosophical defence of the minimal state — the case that even granting individuals' rights, a night-watchman state can still arise legitimately.
Mahatma Gandhi's Dandi March, invoked as a historical anchor: the salt-tax levels that triggered an independence movement were modest compared with what independent India quietly extracts today.

'Mustache allowance,' 'sandstone elephants,' 'policing parrots,' 'golf buggies for the army' — items from Amit's India Uncut catalogue of state spending, used as comic shorthand for the moral cost of unjustified violence-funded expenditure.
Pune as 'the Oxford of the East' — an older Indian intellectual identity invoked to set up the Pune Public Policy Festival sponsor read.
Amit and Ajay on themselves: 'We are all turtles on the march of knowledge towards the end of history.'
